Theodore Roosevelt. The 26th President of the United States and a transformative figure of the Progressive Era. He ascended to the presidency following McKinley's assassination in 1901 and served until 1909, pioneering trust-busting, conservation, and an aggressive foreign policy rooted in American imperial ambition.

Roosevelt became president at 42, the youngest person ever to assume the office. He was known for his vigorous personality, his cowboy past, and his "strenuous life" philosophy. He launched massive antitrust suits against large corporations, earning the nickname "trust-buster." He dissolved the Northern Securities Company and challenged Standard Oil. He established the Panama Canal by supporting Panamanian independence from Colombia and securing canal rights. The canal became the signature engineering achievement of his presidency.

He created the Panama Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine, asserting U.S. right to intervene in Latin American affairs for "hemispheric stability," justifying military occupations across the region. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906 for mediating an end to the Russo-Japanese War, becoming the first American to receive the honor.

Roosevelt founded the conservation movement. He established five national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 federal bird reserves, and four national game preserves, protecting approximately 230 million acres of public land.

He left office in 1909 and became disillusioned with his successor, William Howard Taft. He challenged Taft for the 1912 Republican nomination, lost, and split the party by forming the Progressive, or "Bull Moose," Party. His third-party run split the Republican vote, allowing Democrat Woodrow Wilson to win with only 42 percent of the popular vote, a powerful legacy of intra-party division.
